passages.t: Judah first, and the line to David
passages.happening:
‘These were the sons of Israel’ (verse 1): the twelve sons of Jacob are named in one breath (verses 1-2). Then the chapter turns at once to Judah. His sons Er, Onan and Shelah were born to Bath-shua the Canaanite, and ‘Er, Judah’s firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the LORD, who put him to death’ (verse 3). Tamar bears him Perez and Zerah (verse 4).

In the line of Zerah stands ‘Achar, who brought trouble upon Israel by violating the ban on devoted things’ (verse 7). Then the line of Hezron's son Ram runs through Amminadab, Nahshon, Salmon and Boaz to Obed and Jesse (verses 10-12). Jesse's sons are listed by order of birth, ending, ‘Ozem sixth, and David seventh’ (verse 15). Their sisters Zeruiah and Abigail are named too, and Abigail's son Amasa had an Ishmaelite father (verses 16-17).
passages.hearers:
Judah comes first, though he was Jacob's fourth son, because Judah is the tribe of David, and David is where the book is going. In the middle of this long list stands the line from Ram to Boaz to Jesse and then to David. Everything in the chapter is arranged around that name, which appears here for the first time.

The names come from earlier books: Genesis for Judah's sons, Ruth 4 for the line from Perez to David, Joshua 7 for Achan, and 1 Samuel for David's brothers. The Chronicler spells the thief's name Achar, which sounds like the Hebrew for trouble, so that his name says what he did. The word for his sin, ma'al, breaking faith with God, is one of the book's key words; it will explain Saul's fall and Judah's exile.

The royal line is not presented as spotless. A firstborn put to death, a son born to Tamar in a story of deceit, a thief who troubled Israel. It is presented as chosen. And it is open: Judah's first wife was a Canaanite, and Amasa's father was an Ishmaelite.
passages.later: Matthew begins Jesus' family with this line: ‘Judah was the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar, Perez the father of Hezron, and Hezron the father of Ram’ (Matthew 1:3). Hebrews says, ‘For it is clear that our Lord descended from Judah’ (Hebrews 7:14).
passages.hard:
Was David the seventh son of Jesse, as here, or the eighth, as 1 Samuel says?

Verses 13 to 15 name seven sons of Jesse and call David the seventh. First Samuel 16:10-11 and 17:12 say that Jesse had eight sons, with David the youngest. Readers account for it in a few ways. A common view is that one of the brothers died young or without descendants and was left out of a genealogy that records the lines that went on. Some add that ancient genealogies were often shaped around meaningful numbers, and seven was a number of fullness, so that placing David seventh honors him. Others suggest that one of the eight in Samuel was a relative counted with the household. The Bible does not settle it, and the two accounts agree on what matters to both: David was the youngest of Jesse's sons, chosen over his older brothers.
passages.asks: The line to David runs through a Canaanite wife, Tamar's story and a troubler of Israel. Ask what it means that God works through families like that. And ask what in your own family's story you have kept hidden that God may still use.

passages.t: The clans of Caleb and Jerahmeel
passages.happening: The rest of the chapter sets out the large clans of Caleb and Jerahmeel, Hezron's other sons, and their towns in the hill country of Judah (verses 18-55). Among them is Sheshan, who had no sons, only daughters, ‘but he did have an Egyptian servant named Jarha’ (verse 34). ‘Sheshan gave his daughter in marriage to his servant Jarha, and she bore to him Attai’ (verse 35), and the line goes on for thirteen generations. The chapter closes with the clans of scribes and the Kenites linked to the house of Rechab (verse 55).
passages.hearers:
These lists are found nowhere else in the Bible, and the Chronicler must have had other records. The clans lived in the southern hill country and the Negev. The Jerahmeelites appear as a group in the south in 1 Samuel, and the Calebites were linked with Hebron, which Joshua gave to Caleb son of Jephunneh. How that famous Caleb relates to Caleb son of Hezron here is not certain.

Many names here are towns, among them Tekoa, Ziph, Mareshah, Hebron, Beth-zur, Kiriath-jearim and Bethlehem, each said to have a father, meaning a founder or leading family. For readers in the Persian period some of these lay in their small province, and others, Hebron among them, lay to the south in land then largely held by Edomites. Naming them remembered what the whole tribe had once been.

A family without a son was in danger of losing its name and land. Sheshan's line went on through his daughter and an Egyptian servant who became his son-in-law.
passages.later: Ruth ends with the same line, ‘Obed was the father of Jesse, and Jesse was the father of David’ (Ruth 4:22): a Moabite woman, too, stands in the family of the king.
passages.asks: A servant from Egypt became the ancestor of thirteen generations. Ask whom you have counted out of God's family because of where they came from. And ask what it would mean to give someone a place they had no claim to.
